entries.name: Dakuten
entries.sub: Two dashes that voice the consonant: k→g, s→z, t→d, h→b.

entries.name: Handakuten
entries.sub: A small circle that turns h into p, and lands on no other row.

entries.name: Small っ
entries.sub: This is not a sound of its own. It doubles the consonant that follows. きて / きって.

entries.name: Small ゃ ゅ ょ
entries.sub: Fuse onto the i-row kana in front of them to make ONE syllable.

entries.name: Long vowels
entries.sub: Hold a vowel a beat longer and it is a different word: ー in katakana, a doubled vowel in hiragana.

entries.name: Iteration mark
entries.sub: Repeats the kanji before it. 時 → 時々.

entries.name: Rendaku
entries.sub: Join two words and the second word's first sound often changes: て + かみ → てがみ.

entries.name: Punctuation
entries.sub: How a Japanese sentence is punctuated: 。 、 「 」 ・ 〜, and no spaces.

entries.name: Okurigana
entries.sub: The kana tail written after a kanji, part of the word: 生きる, 高い, 一つ.

entries.name: Conditional sentences
entries.sub: Japanese usually puts the “if” part before what happens next.

entries.name: Because / so
entries.sub: Japanese usually gives the reason before what happened because of it.

entries.name: Must / have to
entries.sub: Japanese puts the action before the words that mean “must” or “have to.”

entries.name: Te-form links and helpers
entries.sub: A te-form can connect an action to extra meaning at the end.

entries.name: Want to / easy / hard
entries.sub: Japanese adds “want to,” “easy,” or “hard” directly after the action.

entries.name: Giving and receiving
entries.sub: The ending shows who does something for whom.

entries.name: I think / seems like
entries.sub: Japanese puts the basic statement before words like “I think” or “might.”

entries.name: Even though / without
entries.sub: Japanese puts the first situation before the main thing that happened.

entries.name: Requests and proposals
entries.sub: Japanese puts the action before the ending that makes it a request or suggestion.

entries.name: Kana
entries.sub: The two Japanese sound scripts, hiragana and katakana, together.

entries.name: Hiragana
entries.sub: The rounded kana, used for Japanese words and grammar.

entries.name: Katakana
entries.sub: The angular kana, used mostly for borrowed words.

entries.name: Romaji
entries.sub: Japanese written in the Latin letters used for English.

entries.name: Kanji
entries.sub: Characters borrowed from Chinese, each carrying a meaning.

entries.name: Kun’yomi and on’yomi
entries.sub: The native Japanese and borrowed Chinese readings of a kanji.

entries.name: Radical
entries.sub: A building block that kanji are made from and filed under.

entries.name: Furigana
entries.sub: Small kana printed next to a kanji to show how it is read.

entries.name: JLPT
entries.sub: A standard test of Japanese, graded N5 (easiest) to N1 (hardest).

entries.name: Dakuten
entries.sub: The two small strokes that voice a kana, turning か into が.

entries.name: Handakuten
entries.sub: The small circle that turns the は row into p sounds.

entries.name: Yōon
entries.sub: A small や, ゆ or よ joined to an i row kana, like きゃ.

entries.name: Okurigana
entries.sub: The kana tail written after a kanji, like the る in 見る.

entries.name: Rendaku
entries.sub: Voicing that appears when two words join, like て plus かみ giving てがみ.

entries.name: Counter
entries.sub: A word added to a number to count a kind of thing, like 本 or 人.

entries.name: Particle
entries.sub: A small word that marks another word's job in the sentence, like は, を or へ.

entries.name: Keigo
entries.sub: Polite Japanese, split into honorific language and humble language.

entries.name: Pitch accent
entries.sub: The rise and fall in a word that can tell two look-alike words apart.

entries.name: Mora
entries.sub: A unit of timing, the single beat that most kana take.

entries.name: Verb types
entries.sub: Every verb is one of two groups (with some exceptions), and the group decides how every form is built.

entries.name: い-adjectives and な-adjectives
entries.sub: い-adjectives conjugate themselves; な-adjectives take な and lean on です for tense and connection.

entries.name: Keigo: the politeness levels
entries.sub: Three registers: polite, honorific for the other person, humble for yourself.

entries.name: Numbers 11–99
entries.sub: Past ten, you build numbers instead of memorizing them.

entries.name: Hundreds and up
entries.sub: The big steps are their own words. Everything between builds from them.
